A1.justification: Both PDFs describe E2EDev and provide readable methods, experiments, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Their shared content can be matched reliably despite extensive reformatting and added evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original framework evaluations on E2EDev, human annotation and error analyses, and HumanEval/HumanEval-ET experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds Claude-Haiku 4.5 results, OpenHands/SWE-Agent comparisons, and an expanded annotation reliability audit.

M1.justification: The proposed HITL-MAA workflow retains test-ID annotation, requirement extraction, Gherkin scenario generation, Python implementation, iterative verification, and human fallback. Algorithms 1–2 and the annotation prompts in Appendix G preserve the same procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 46 web projects, 244 requirements, and 703 BDD scenarios, alongside HumanEval and HumanEval-ET. The additional models and agents are evaluated on retained tasks; newly discussed benchmarks are not added evaluation datasets.

E2.justification: v3 adds OpenHands and SWE-Agent to the E2EDev comparisons for GPT-4o and Claude-Haiku 4.5 (Appendix C.1, Table 8). These materially broaden the comparison to general-purpose coding agents alongside the six retained methods. HumanEval comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds the Claude-Haiku 4.5 backbone and specifies adapted operating conditions for OpenHands and SWE-Agent. Appendix B.1 also replaces the stated Vanilla LLM output-format instructions with an H5-developer prompt. Human evaluation reportedly expands from 300 to 360 projects, although Appendix B.3 retains the old 295-instance remainder, leaving allocation unclear.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2.2 adds a blind reliability audit of 100 stratified test cases by ten evaluators, including five additional external experts, to check agreement beyond the original annotation team. Existing failure-mode analyses, ChatDev interaction analysis, and calculator case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 gives main benchmark point estimates without specifying repeated-run counts or standard deviations. v3 specifies three effectiveness runs per task and reports means with standard deviations in Tables 3 and 8, substantially improving uncertainty reporting. Efficiency is explicitly single-run, and OpenHands rows lack standard deviations; v1's run count remains unspecified.

E6.justification: v3 adds Claude-Haiku 4.5 and OpenHands/SWE-Agent results, Claude soft-requirement scores, and the audit agreement of 0.81. Most main-table effectiveness values are replaced by three-run summaries: GPT-Engineer/GPT-4o requirement accuracy changes from 50.37% to 50.83% ±1.33. This is revised aggregation, not an established performance gain. HumanEval/HumanEval-ET results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 retains the accuracy definitions, Balanced Score weights of 0.6 and 0.4, and cost/carbon equations. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the fine-grained BDD benchmark, automated evaluation, and HITL-MAA construction framework. Both versions conclude that detailed requirement fulfillment remains difficult and multi-agent coordination often adds considerable cost with limited benefit. The Claude example extends support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit scope arguments concerning web applications and exclusion of CI/CD and deep backend inspection, and qualifies the adapted OpenHands/SWE-Agent comparisons. It also shifts the explanation of UI-detail errors toward dilution of constraints between agents and clarifies MetaGPT's untuned HumanEval comparison.

D1.justification: v3 documents implementation adaptations for the new agents, annotator recruitment and participation conditions, and CC-BY 4.0 data/MIT code licensing. Existing code and dataset access links, testing instructions, and detailed HITL-MAA prompts were already provided in v1.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Table 1 refocus the comparison on repository-level benchmarks, adding GitTaskBench and Mle-Bench while removing function-level rows. OpenHands, SWE-Agent, and several other works are newly cited. The central positioning around BDD-based requirement verification remains intact.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, construction narrative, and failure analysis undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Project-selection details move into Appendix A.1, project features join Section 3.1, and the conclusion, limitations, ethics, and LLM-usage disclosures are reorganized.

P2.justification: The paper is comprehensively reformatted into two columns. The introductory figures are combined and redrawn, result tables add standard-deviation displays and comparison colors, and new agent-results and task-formulation tables appear. Existing figures, tables, and code listings are extensively resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: Three-run uncertainty reporting, the broader expert audit, and documented additional comparisons make the empirical claims easier to assess. These gains are limited by reporting inconsistencies: Appendix B.3 retains 295 remaining instances despite increasing the total to 360, and Table 10 reports a Claude/ChatDev delta of 0.2718 although 0.7025 minus 0.4464 equals 0.2561. Overall, the added evidence and transparency provide a bounded net improvement.
